title: Episodic tenant credits, predictive autoscale, and transparent degradation for GPU fleet isolation
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Goal: implement a hybrid tenant isolation mechanism that combines short-lived "episodic credits" with a predictive autoscaler and deterministic graceful-degradation behaviours to meet per-tenant throughput guarantees while minimizing noisy neighbor impact.

Background: customers on Dedicated require predictable throughput SLOs. Current coarse hard-slicing and soft-eviction approaches either waste capacity or allow occasional noisy neighbors to cause tail-latency spikes. We need a solution that enforces per-tenant contracts, allows benign burstiness, and degrades predictably when capacity is constrained.

High-level proposal: 1) Episodic tenant credits: each tenant has a token bucket-like credit pool that accrues slowly (sustained baseline) plus episodic top-ups for contracted burst windows. Credits are consumed by allocation units (GPU-lane-seconds). When credits are low, the tenant transitions through controlled degradation states (reduced batch sizes, lower-priority scheduling, or fallback to smaller model variants).

2) Predictive autoscaler: use short-window traffic forecasting (5–60s) + GPU utilization signals to preemptively spin up reserved micro-lanes or invoke burst pool capacity. Forecasting model runs in the control-plane, emits confidence scores; when confidence high, autoscaler creates ephemeral reservation slices to keep latency SLOs.

3) Noisy neighbor scoring ('opacity score'): continuous distributed detector that correlates request-level metrics (p99 latency spikes, KV cache eviction churn, GPU SM utilization bursts, memory pressure) into a noise score per tenant. High-score tenants are subject to immediate mitigation (credit burn penalty, temporary throttles, or eviction to best-effort pool) and flagged for operator review.

4) Transparent degradation and observability: expose degradation state and remaining credits via the Console API and per-tenant dashboard, with clear user-facing reasons (e.g., "credit-depleted: autoscale delayed") and recommended remediation. Include an incident playbook for noisy tenant remediation and customer communications.

Design trade-offs: 
- Credit-based approach increases bookkeeping overhead and requires fast consistent counters; we choose eventually-consistent local caches with periodic reconciliation to avoid tail latency amplification.
- Predictive autoscaler reduces false evictions but may increase short-term cost due to overprovisioning; mitigation: confidence threshold and cost cap per tenant.
- Degradation modes must preserve core correctness of API responses; prefer model-variant fallback over dropping tokens for high-value customers.

Metrics and success criteria: preserve 99th-percentile latency SLO for P1 tenants under 95th percentile load events, reduce noisy-neighbor-induced p99 spikes by >=60% on pilot fleet, and show <8% additional capacity reserved for predictive autoscaler on average.

Implementation plan: 
- Phase 1 (spike & prototype): implement credit ledger prototype and local caching; build simple noise score ruleset.
- Phase 2 (integration): wire predictive autoscaler, implement mitigation actions, and surface state in Console.
- Phase 3 (pilot): run with 10 pilot tenants on a single region Dedicated fleet, measure outcomes, iterate.

Acceptance tests: unit tests for credit accounting, e2e with synthetic load (bursty + sustained), and fault-injection for reconciliation gaps.
acceptance_criteria: Per-tenant credit accounting is implemented and passes unit tests for accrual/consumption/reconciliation
Predictive autoscaler can instantiate ephemeral reservations within configured SLAs and respects per-tenant cost caps
Noisy neighbor detector reduces observed tenant-induced p99 latency spikes by >=60% in pilot
